title: Scalable Multi-Action Offline Policy Learning with an $m$-ary Tree

problem.claim: Offline policy-learning methods must represent complex treatment heterogeneity and scale to industrial datasets with tens of millions of observations.

gap.claim: Binary policy trees may be too restrictive, while existing tree-search algorithms may not scale to industrial-sized datasets.

contributions.claim: A scalable offline policy-learning method for multi-action settings using fixed-depth, bounded-branching m-ary policy trees.
The method exactly optimizes policy trees on categorical or discretized features by maximizing an estimated policy value based on doubly robust scores.
The method combines pruning, caching, and parallelization to improve scalability, and uses nested folds to leverage all observations for statistical efficiency.

author_reported_evidence.claim: In 7 of 20 industry-scale experiments, m-ary policy trees surpassed a commonly used policy assigning the same globally winning action to everyone after false-discovery-rate adjustment.
At greater depth, globally optimized binary trees still do not produce comparable gains.

narrative_sequence.summary: Decision trees are used as interpretable policies for personalized treatment assignment.
Binary trees may lack expressiveness and existing tree-search methods may not scale to industrial datasets.
The authors introduce an offline multi-action policy-learning method that exactly optimizes bounded-depth m-ary trees using doubly robust policy-value estimates.
Multiway splits improve expressiveness, while pruning, caching, parallelization, and nested folds address scalability and statistical efficiency.
The authors report gains over a global-winner-for-all policy in seven of 20 experiments, whereas deeper globally optimized binary trees do not show comparable gains.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the number of actions, tree depths, or branching factors evaluated.
The abstract does not identify the industry domains, datasets, or baselines beyond the global-winner-for-all policy and binary trees.
The abstract does not report computational-resource requirements or absolute performance values.
